title: AI made game dev possible for me, can’t tell if that’s special or just the new default
author: JoseQuanGT
selftext:
I only recently started making games. AI is pretty much the reason I could start at all.

Describe an idea (retro starship/mecha space combat) and its playable in minutes. Then just iterate from there… feels crazy.

BUT, if AI is magical… what happens when everyone has access to the same magic?

How are you deciding what’s worth finishing vs just another project for urself?

comments.author: Bluetails_Buizel
comments.body: Well, it is harder to sell/ market it

replies.author: JoseQuanGT
replies.body: Do u think AI can also help there?

replies.author: Bluetails_Buizel
replies.body: For advertising? No? You still have to pay money to host your ads there. Maybe you can get creative on ads, maybe. (Most of them looks like obvious ai slop anyway)

replies.author: satupidfukignidot
replies.body: Vast majority of us GenZers cannot afford to hire employees under any circumstances. Even if we go to the SEA or IND regions, working with a single employee for 1 day a week would put over 70% of us on the street.

replies.author: Bluetails_Buizel
replies.body: I can feel, I don’t get why westerners have high standards when it comes to art, smh, I wish we can get an audience from there. Even China social media is locked down we can’t advertise our products there.

replies.author: satupidfukignidot
replies.body:
To be fair, there's a LOT more potential in the tool than oneshot T2I slop. If someone can tell you used AI... that's a skill issue on your part. It's a powerful tool, not an excuse to turn off your brain.

If you've not tried learning Krita Diffusion or ComfyUI, and are a fan of AI artistic tooling; try them you will love them when you get the hang of it (provided you have at least 8GB of VRAM).

replies.author: flavorgenerator
replies.body: It's really not that helpful, because it can have great ideas, but getting eyes on anything is the hard part

replies.author: Live_Length_5814
replies.body: Most of the internet is bots so yes

replies.author: JoseQuanGT
replies.body: Do u think AI bots will curate games for their humans???  Maybe start optimizing messaging to AI bots/agents

replies.author: Live_Length_5814
replies.body: They already do.

replies.author: EchoingAngel
replies.body: Marketing is extremely hard and AI has been really bad at writing good copy. I say this as someone that really wished it was good at it, but any text in/around your game longer than 2 words needs hands on attention. Astra helped a ton to clean up Sol AI slop writing, but it's still not good enough to sell things.

replies.author: JoseQuanGT
replies.body: AI tends to output average copy… the worst if u want to stand out

replies.author: KHRZ
replies.body: I found 500 gaming press emails to send press kit/pitch email with GPT. 1% of them made articles, and those very minor and/or AI slop websites. So while in theory it could work, they are probably already drowned in spam.

comments.author: willjameswaltz
comments.body: As a professional gamedev (animation mostly), I saw a lot of technologies come and go before I left the industry. Mocap was the big moment for us animators "will traditional animation die?" the answer is, that games just get bigger. After all the initial lay-offs and excitement dies down and people actually have used the innovative tools to actually make something good, things just get bigger, everyone gets new jobs, things evolve. Look at GTA VI. Gigantic game, took forever. Now with ai-assisted tools all along the production line, the next game will be 10x, 100x larger and take just as long to build. You'll get approximations that use the new technologies to cut corners, but ultimately, AAA will stay AAA, AA and A will stay AA and A, everything will just have a new layer of baseline complexity.

replies.author: JoseQuanGT
replies.body: So use AI to make even browser games bigger… right?

replies.author: Pure-Masterpiece-857
replies.body: Naw. Use it to make something you really love, and then replace the bits that don't work with handmade stuff. Expect the third half of development to take the longest.

replies.author: Tkwan777
replies.body:
This is my experience. It gets me to a starting point where I have a usable base, but AI doesnt have my vision, so I have to make a Lot of adjustments.

AI is double edged. It allowed easier access to tools for everyone, so we will get a lot more slop. But it still takes people with vision and an artistic eye to create something good. So, sure there will be lots of slop produced now that AI has lowered the barrier to entry, but gems will shine through.

comments.author: shlaifu
comments.body: 10 bucks you can still spot the assetflip/slop for the foreseeable future. After that - welcome to why every designer on the planet has fallen into depression.

comments.author: flavorgenerator
comments.body: It's the new default and you're ahead of the curve because you're using it and are on r/aigamedev. It absolutely is magical and now anyone can vibe code a prototype game in literally hours, that would have taken weeks or months before AI. Now everything is about actually coming up with something new, working super hard to polish it and make it beyond just vibe coded prototypes, and the hardest one, finding people who actually want to play it in a sea of thousands of other games

replies.author: Time_Cat_5212
replies.body:
Getting from the vibe coded "prototype" to a spec driven work in progress, something fully thought out with a clear plan that can actually be built into a real game, seems to be the inflection point.

I think there was a moment when these quick demos were like "wow" and someone might actually try it, treat it like a real thing that might go somewhere, but that window is closing.  I think the bar is higher now, even for incomplete drafts and early versions.

replies.author: JoseQuanGT
replies.body: Yes, feel like the bar is exponentially getting higher by the day

comments.author: TheNasky1
comments.body: It's special if you make something Good and people buy it. Otherwise you're just sheep

comments.author: _raydeStar
comments.body:
Blunt answer -- you're competing against people with industry experience who know what they are doing. 

I have a coworker that scaffolds up production-grade games in a week or two, because that's what he does.  

What you lack is \*experience\*.  it feels like a magic wonderland, but there is still a lot of work to be done.  figure out what that is, and fill the knowledge gaps.  

You are not too late, too early, or anything.  What you ARE is in the 'slush pile' where everything goes to die. Distinguish yourself through persistent work, and you'll have a breakthrough, but it is not going to be a 'hehe weekend project' thing.  It is going to take a sickening amount of effort, and you have to be ready to pay the price.

replies.author: sicospecialist
replies.body: Totally agree, ive been coding, learned every aspect of production, from c#, 3D asset workflows from start to finish, all old school by hand. Now with Ai, it makes things smoother, easier and faster, but without the experience, it would be total Dog poo. My sister works at MS on Mincraft and other projects, they now use Ai. With the knowledge, you guide Ai not depend on it. Its a tool, like for instance Substance painter when it came around, made Photoshop kinda redundant for hand making textures.

replies.author: _raydeStar
replies.body:
I am only a game dev by hobby, but I am also a professional software dev.  There is still a clear disparity between a seasoned dev and a vibe coder.  

That is not saying 'don't vibe code', but I AM saying if you want to make it, you are going to have to leverage AI to up your skillset.

replies.author: sicospecialist
replies.body: 1000% correct, I think it will more people understand the inner workings and maybe want to learn the craft as well.

comments.author: MidSerpent
comments.body:
I’m too ambitious to just “describe an idea and it’s playable in minutes.”

I get into the idea stage every damn time I start coming up with features that require some sort of software tech that doesn’t really exist for game development now.

Then is set off to build that tech and open source it instead.

But in coming at it from a different position from you. I make games professionally, what AI has done for me is let me have enough time for side projects.

replies.author: JoseQuanGT
replies.body: From feature creep to project creep

replies.author: MidSerpent
replies.body: Other people ship games, I ship open source machine learning libraries designed and engineers to be used in game engines…

comments.author: CapitalDiligent1676
comments.body: Don't worry, it's normal, you remain incompetent... do everything with your subscription

comments.author: Seerix
comments.body:
I've made a ton of prototypes. None of them were very interesting or fun. Until the last one I made... realized I was still messing around with it after an hour, and I had a huge list of ideas I wanted to implement, then I could see how the systems would mesh together to create a gameplay loop, and now i've used about 3 weeks of tokens on my $100 codex sub since sunday afternoon. It's coming together pretty well!   
  
Quickest and easiest way to describe it is: starsector with crew first controls meets Xcom (meets rimworld colonist npcs kinda, the crew are a lot more detailed than xcom squad members, and you'll have to feed and equip them.) Salvaging wrecks, exploring derelicts and asteroid fields, ship to ship combat, fully modular shipbuilding, 2.5D isometric

replies.author: JoseQuanGT
replies.body: Sounds ambitious… 💪

replies.author: Seerix
replies.body: Yep. Good chance I dont finish it. That's okay though, im having tons of fun

comments.author: Square-Yam-3772
comments.body:
you mean, like, what happened for the last 2-3 years? lol

it is not all that different for indie dev tbh: it was hard to market/sell games, it is still hard (probably harder) to market/sell games. 

it is still new to you but it is not a new situation for many of us. Even before AI, game engines and templates make it really easy to make playable games 

imo, it has been the same trend for the \~15-20 years(just spitballing here): gamedev gets easier, more people make games and people complain about not getting players.
